title: Functionally homologous representation of vocalizations in the auditory cortex of humans and macaques.
abstract: How the evolution of speech has transformed the human auditory cortex compared to other primates remains largely unknown. While primary auditory cortex is organized largely similarly in humans and macaques,<sup>1</sup> the picture is much less clear at higher levels of the anterior auditory pathway,<sup>2</sup> particularly regarding the processing of conspecific vocalizations (CVs). A "voice region" similar to the human voice-selective areas<sup>3</sup><sup>,</sup><sup>4</sup> has been identified in the macaque right anterior temporal lobe with functional MRI;<sup>5</sup> however, its anatomical localization, seemingly inconsistent with that of the human temporal voice areas (TVAs), has suggested a "repositioning of the voice area" in recent human evolution.<sup>6</sup> Here we report a functional homology in the cerebral processing of vocalizations by macaques and humans, using comparative fMRI and a condition-rich auditory stimulation paradigm. We find that the anterior temporal lobe of both species possesses cortical voice areas that are bilateral and not only prefer conspecific vocalizations but also implement a representational geometry categorizing them apart from all other sounds in a species-specific but homologous manner. These results reveal a more similar functional organization of higher-level auditory cortex in macaques and humans than currently known.
